questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a research question from a broad topic
questions.stem: A cooling design brief opens with the topic 'battery thermal management'. Which revision states a research question?

options.text: Does more cooling-plate airflow lower peak cell temperature during a 30-minute discharge?
What subject area covers the cooling of battery packs?
options.misconception: Confuses a subject area with a focused, answerable question

options.text: Why is battery thermal management worth researching at all?
options.misconception: Asks why the field matters rather than posing a claim

options.text: What is the general topic of battery thermal systems?
options.misconception: Repeats the topic in question form without narrowing it

questions.explanation: A research question names a specific relationship and a measurable outcome. The other three restate the topic or its importance without saying what would be compared.
questions.hint: Ask what would be compared and what outcome recorded.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Separate a hypothesis from the research question it motivates
questions.stem: An engineer writes the hypothesis 'increasing fan speed raises board temperature'. Which statement captures the matching research question?

options.text: How does mean board temperature change when fan speed rises from 20 to 60 percent?
Why does the board become hot when the fan is slowed down?
options.misconception: Reverses the direction of the relationship in the hypothesis

options.text: Is fan speed an interesting variable to study in this enclosure?
options.misconception: Names a variable instead of asking about a measured effect

options.text: Does higher fan speed cause the board to heat up, in general terms?
options.misconception: Keeps the causal wording vague and specifies no comparison

questions.explanation: The hypothesis predicts a direction of effect and the research question asks for that effect to be measured. A usable question fixes the manipulation and the outcome, which the vague options never do.
questions.hint: The question must be answerable by measurement, not belief.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a claim can be shown false
questions.stem: A design brief lists five claims: 'the alloy stretches less under the same load', 'the coating wears out sooner', 'the coating is a more elegant colour', 'the bracket is easier to assemble', and 'the bracket is the finest design ever'. How many of the five are falsifiable in principle?
questions.explanation: Three claims name measurable properties: strain, wear life and assembly effort. Colour elegance and 'finest ever' have no observation that could count against them, so neither can be falsified.
questions.hint: A claim is falsifiable if some result could prove it wrong.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Turn a loose attribute into an operational definition
questions.stem: In a design brief, 'better grip' is used as the key attribute of a new handle. Write an operational definition for 'better grip' that another engineer could repeat.

answer.exemplar: Define better grip as the mean of three measurements of the friction coefficient between a gloved fingertip and the handle surface, taken with a calibrated pull tester at 20 N normal force, where a higher mean means better grip.

questions.explanation: An operational definition names what is measured, how, and under what conditions. 'Better grip' alone leaves the unit, instrument and procedure to the observer, so two engineers would score it differently.
questions.hint: Name the measurement, the instrument and the conditions.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Assign independent and dependent roles to variables
questions.stem: A design brief studies a fibre-reinforced panel: panel thickness is varied and the peak load at failure is recorded. Which labelling is correct?

options.text: Thickness is the independent variable and peak failure load is the dependent variable
Peak failure load is the independent variable and thickness is the dependent one
options.misconception: Swaps the manipulated variable with the recorded outcome

options.text: Both quantities are independent because neither is deliberately manipulated
options.misconception: Treats a recorded outcome as though it were manipulated

options.text: Both quantities are dependent because each is read while the other varies
options.misconception: Assumes every variable must be dependent by definition

questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one the engineer deliberately changes, here panel thickness. The dependent variable is the outcome that responds and is recorded, here the peak load at failure.
questions.hint: Ask which one you set and which one you measure.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Recognise confounders in a design

stimulus.body: Two prototype ovens were compared. Oven A used a recycled steel liner and a reused door seal, while oven B used a new stainless liner and a fresh seal. The rebuilt oven baked a loaf in 41 minutes and the older oven in 36 minutes.

questions.stem: Using the brief excerpt, which variable confounds the comparison of baking time between the two ovens?

options.text: The liner and seal materials differ between the two ovens as well
The ambient room temperature during each test
options.misconception: Treats a shared background condition as the cause of the gap

options.text: The number of loaves baked in each oven before measurement
options.misconception: Blames prior use rather than the hardware difference

options.text: The type of flour used for the loaf in the later trial
options.misconception: Blames a factor that was identical in both trial runs

questions.explanation: A confounder differs between the groups and could explain the gap. The liner and seal materials differ between the ovens, so the timing gap cannot be credited to rebuild status alone.
questions.hint: Look for what else changed between the two cases.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Specify the controls a study needs
questions.stem: A design brief compares a new damping coating against the standard one. First the engineers add untreated sample panels as controls. Then they test one coated and one uncoated panel in the same rig. Which setup provides the strongest control?

options.text: Untreated panels held and tested under identical rig conditions, isolating the coating effect
Coated panels tested in a hotter rig so the coating is clearly exercised
options.misconception: Alters rig conditions, so the coating effect is not isolated

options.text: Untreated panels stored on the bench while the coated panel is tested
options.misconception: Stores controls unused, so they cannot detect any rig effect

options.text: Both panel types tested but with different rig settings to reflect real use
options.misconception: Varies rig settings between arms, confounding the comparison

questions.explanation: Controls must match the treatment on everything except the factor being tested, and go through the same procedure. Stored panels and mismatched rig settings each add differences of their own.
questions.hint: A control should differ in one way only: the treatment.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain what randomisation protects against
questions.stem: A design brief tests three surface finishes on twenty identical coupons. What does randomly assigning coupons to finish groups chiefly achieve?

options.text: It spreads pre-existing variation in hardness evenly across the three groups
It guarantees that every coupon in each group is exactly alike
options.misconception: Believes randomisation can make all units physically identical

options.text: It removes the need for a control group of untreated coupons
options.misconception: Thinks randomisation substitutes for a baseline comparison group

options.text: It ensures the finished results are identical between the three groups
options.misconception: Confuses random assignment with identical group outcomes

questions.explanation: Random assignment spreads existing variation evenly across groups so it cannot be mistaken for the finish effect. It does not make units identical, remove the need for controls, or force equal outcomes.
questions.hint: Randomisation balances what you did not control.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a research question from a broad topic
questions.stem: Two engineers write briefs for one project. One asks 'How can we make the pump quieter?' The other asks 'Does replacing the impeller with a six-vane design reduce sound pressure level by at least 3 dB at 1 metre?'. Which brief is researchable?

options.text: The second, because it fixes the change and the measured outcome with a threshold
The first, because open-ended questions allow the broadest exploration
options.misconception: Treats a wish for improvement as a researchable question

options.text: Both, because either wording can be answered once the pump is built
options.misconception: Assumes any wording becomes testable once hardware exists

options.text: Neither, because a research question must avoid naming any measurable outcome
options.misconception: Believes a good question must hide what gets measured

questions.explanation: A researchable question states the change, the outcome and sometimes a threshold. 'Make it quieter' names a goal but not a test, so different teams could read it as asking different things.
questions.hint: Look for a named change and a named measured outcome.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a claim can be shown false
questions.stem: A design brief claims the new alloy 'will work better than steel in every application'. Explain why a reviewer rejects this claim as untestable.

answer.exemplar: The claim is universal and comparative but specifies no measurable property, no application and no threshold, so no observation can count against it. A usable version would name a property, an application and the value that would show the alloy failing.

questions.explanation: Falsifiability requires that some possible observation could count against the claim. 'Every application' admits no counterexample to choose, so the claim cannot be tested and cannot be supported either.
questions.hint: Ask what result would prove the claim wrong.

questions.stem: Four operational definitions for 'tool wear' are proposed in a design brief. Which one is specified enough for another team to replicate it?

options.text: Wear index measured as the change in cutting edge radius in micrometres after 20 minutes
Wear measured as how worn the cutting edge looks after 20 minutes of cutting
options.misconception: Leaves the instrument and metric to personal judgement

options.text: Wear measured on the cutting edge using the standard wear measurement procedure
options.misconception: Cites an unnamed procedure instead of naming measurements

options.text: Wear measured as the loss of cutting edge sharpness using the team's wear scale
options.misconception: Uses a scale with no units, range or calibration stated

questions.explanation: Replication needs a quantity, a unit and a procedure. Option A names the geometric quantity, the unit in micrometres and the cutting condition; the others leave one of those unspecified.
questions.hint: A definition needs a quantity, a unit and a method.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Assign independent and dependent roles to variables

stimulus.body: The team varied the voltage applied to a sensor heater and recorded the drift in the reference reading over one hour. Drift rose from 0.4 mV at 3 volts to 1.9 mV at 9 volts.

questions.stem: Referring to the brief excerpt, which statement correctly identifies the independent and dependent variables?

options.text: Applied voltage is independent and hourly drift in the reading is dependent
Hourly drift is independent and applied voltage is dependent
options.misconception: Reverses the manipulated variable and the recorded response

options.text: Both are independent because the heater power was also logged
options.misconception: Adds a logged variable and loses the cause and effect link

options.text: Neither is independent because the reading changes over the hour
options.misconception: Argues a time trend removes the manipulated variable entirely

questions.explanation: The voltage is set by the team at several levels, so it is the independent variable. The drift is the outcome the team observes and records, so it is the dependent variable.
questions.hint: The set quantity is independent; the response is dependent.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Recognise confounders in a design
questions.stem: A design brief tests a rust-resistant coating. First the engineers coat half the coupons and leave half bare. Then all coupons sit in a salt chamber, but the bare ones are older stock. What should the team do first?

options.text: Reallocate so treated and untreated coupons come from the same batch and age
Increase the salt chamber time so the difference becomes easier to detect
options.misconception: Increases exposure instead of removing the batch confound

options.text: Add more uncoated coupons to make the untreated group statistically larger
options.misconception: Adds sample size while leaving the stock-age confound in place

options.text: Measure coating thickness first and select the thickest coupons for treatment
options.misconception: Selects on thickness, creating a fresh confounder of its own

questions.explanation: Bare coupons differ in batch and age, so coating and stock age vary together and the comparison is confounded. Rebalancing within one batch removes that coupling before replication helps.
questions.hint: Remove the coupling between the treatment and the stock.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Specify the controls a study needs
questions.stem: In a design brief comparing two seal compounds, what is the purpose of running an unmodified seal under the same test rig?

options.text: It provides a baseline for judging how much of the result comes from the rig
It proves that the unmodified seal has no failure mode of its own
options.misconception: Expects a control to be flawless rather than just comparable

options.text: It removes the need to repeat each test condition more than once
options.misconception: Believes a baseline removes the need for repeated measurements

options.text: It demonstrates that both compounds fail in the same way under load
options.misconception: Reads a shared failure mode as proof of equivalent performance

questions.explanation: An unmodified control goes through the same rig so that any effect of the rig itself can be separated from the effect of the compound. It is a baseline for comparison, not a claim of perfection.
questions.hint: A control shows what the apparatus alone produces.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain what randomisation protects against
questions.stem: Twelve brackets are sorted by measured stiffness, then a table of random numbers assigns six to the new finish and six to the old finish. What does this assignment achieve?

options.text: It spreads the stiffest and softest brackets across both finish groups roughly evenly
It guarantees that each finish group contains exactly the same bracket stiffness
options.misconception: Assumes a random table alone produces perfectly matched groups

options.text: It proves that the finish has no effect on stiffness once the table is applied
options.misconception: Treats randomisation as proof that the treatment had no effect

options.text: It removes the need to measure bracket stiffness at all before assignment
options.misconception: Believes randomisation removes the need for baseline measurement

questions.explanation: Random assignment spreads any pre-existing stiffness difference across groups instead of aligning it with the finish. It promises neither perfect balance nor any particular outcome.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Separate a hypothesis from the research question it motivates
questions.stem: A brief states: 'If the flange is ground to a finer finish, torque ripple will fall by 15 percent.' Explain how this statement relates to a research question.

answer.exemplar: The statement is a directional hypothesis: it predicts a specific change of 15 percent in a named outcome under a named condition. A research question would ask what the measured torque ripple actually is under that condition, so the two are complementary rather than interchangeable.

questions.explanation: A hypothesis commits to a predicted direction and size; the research question asks what is actually observed. The hypothesis sets the expectation against which the question's answer is judged.
questions.hint: One predicts an outcome; the other asks for it.

Steel is finest; the finish looks premium; the bracket is stronger; brake torque falls 12 percent

stimulus.body: The brief asks whether the new surface finish reduces grip loss after 500 handling cycles. Grip is described only as 'how well it grips'. The test team proposes a five-point rating scale.

Adding the word 'good' before grip so the attribute reads more positively

options.misconception: Uses a subjective scale instead of a measured quantity

options.misconception: Collects descriptions rather than operationalising the attribute

questions.explanation: An operational definition turns an attribute into a measurement another person could repeat. Ratings and descriptions leave the score to the observer, while a force in newtons is checkable.

questions.stem: A brief tests a damping compound. First the team sets the shaker frequency to a fixed 50 hertz. Then it varies the compound thickness and records the peak acceleration of the housing. Which labelling fits?

Thickness is the dependent variable because the shaker responds to the compound
options.misconception: Treats the varied factor as the outcome instead of the fixed one

options.text: Peak acceleration is the independent variable because it is measured first each run
options.misconception: Confuses the order of measurement with the causal direction

options.text: Frequency and thickness are both independent while acceleration is neither
options.misconception: Leaves the recorded outcome without any variable role at all

questions.learningObjective: Recognise confounders in a design
questions.stem: In a design brief, a new welding flux is credited with producing joints of higher tensile strength. Which situation would weaken that claim most?

options.text: The flux joints were also annealed, while the comparison joints were not
Both joint types were pulled to failure on the same testing machine
options.misconception: Confuses a shared testing condition with a source of bias

options.text: Ten joints of each type were tested and the averages were reported
options.misconception: Mistakes a reasonable sample size for evidence of confounding

options.text: The tensile test followed the same procedure the team wrote earlier
options.misconception: Reads a standard test procedure as a cause of joint strength

questions.stem: A design brief sets out three comparison groups for a paint durability test: a new formulation, an old formulation and a panel left uncoated as a control. How many groups in the brief are control groups?
questions.explanation: Only the uncoated panel is a control, since it lacks the treatment being tested, while the two formulations are comparison groups of the treatment at different levels. Counting requires separating controls from comparisons.
questions.hint: A control lacks the treatment that is being tested.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain what randomisation protects against
questions.stem: A design brief proposes testing the new joint on the first twelve assemblies built each week. Explain the risk in this arrangement for estimating the new joint's performance.

answer.exemplar: Assigning by build order makes the new joint coincide with whatever conditions happen to occur on the first builds of each week, such as fresh tooling or a particular shift, so any difference could be caused by those. Random assignment within each week breaks that link between treatment and build-time conditions.

questions.explanation: Assigning by build order ties the treatment to whatever varies with time, such as tool wear or shift changes. Random assignment within each week breaks that link.
questions.hint: Ask what else changes with the order of the work.

options.misconception: Ranks the statement about importance above the testable one

questions.explanation: Rankability follows how much a statement commits to, and only the thickness and pressure rating statement fixes both a change and a recordable outcome. The others commit to nothing measurable.

A list of every published paper that also favours composite plates over metal
options.misconception: Gathers supporting literature instead of a refuting condition

options.text: An assertion that no test result has yet contradicted the composite plate claim

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Specify the controls a study needs
questions.stem: A brief compares a new gasket material against a baseline gasket. Explain what could go wrong if the two gaskets are tested on different fixtures of the same design.

answer.exemplar: Fixtures of the same design can differ in machining tolerance, fastener torque and seating behaviour, so the fixture itself could explain part of the difference in leakage. Testing both gaskets on matched fixtures, or on the same fixture in turn, keeps the fixture out of the comparison.

questions.explanation: Control conditions hold everything except the factor under test constant, and two nominally identical fixtures are not constant in practice. Machining or clamping differences can enter the result.
questions.hint: Same design does not mean identical behaviour.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Recognise confounders in a design
questions.stem: A brief credits a new anodising bath with reducing corrosion. The old bath and the new bath differ in temperature, dwell time and concentration. Explain what this means for the credit given to the bath.

answer.exemplar: Three factors differ along with the bath itself, so any corrosion difference could be caused by temperature, dwell time or concentration rather than by the new chemistry. Holding those three settings the same for both baths, or changing one at a time, would let the chemistry be assessed on its own.

questions.explanation: A confound varies with the treatment and could produce the outcome. With temperature, dwell time and concentration all changing, the comparison cannot separate the new chemistry from the settings.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Assign independent and dependent roles to variables
questions.stem: A brief says: 'We raised the pump speed by 400 revolutions per minute and the discharge pressure rose by 6 bar.' Explain how the two quantities should be labelled.

answer.exemplar: Pump speed is the quantity the engineers deliberately changed, so it is the independent variable. Discharge pressure is the response that followed and was measured, so it is the dependent variable, and the direction of change does not affect either label.

questions.explanation: The label depends on what the team did, not on what happened. Speed was set by the engineers and pressure responded and was recorded, so speed is independent and pressure dependent.
